title: The Song We Keep
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 39 of 40
content:
Greg wanted to finish the song on a receipt.

The receipt was from a place that sold car batteries, and the back of it was already covered in a list of things the van needed. He had squeezed four lines of music between BRAKE FLUID and PLEASE REMEMBER TO EAT ACTUAL FOOD.

“Very professional,” I said.

“Hey, some of my best work happened near questionable paperwork.”

“You wrote one of your songs on a parking ticket.”

“And look how that turned out.”

“I don't remember hearing it.”

“Exactly. Nobody can prove it was bad.”

I laughed, and he smiled the way he always did when a joke landed more gently than he'd expected.

It was the last warm week of summer in Beach City. The boardwalk had begun closing earlier, but there were still people in shorts walking past with ice cream melting down their wrists. The wind carried salt and the distant metallic squeal of the amusement rides. Greg had parked near the pier because the car wash was too busy for us to think.

We had been working on the song for a month.

Not a love song exactly. Not a breakup song. Not a list of things we'd survived. It was the sound of learning how to stay without deciding that staying meant never changing.

Every time Greg reached the second verse, he changed the chords.

“Do you hate the verse?” I asked.

“No.”

“Do you hate me?”

He stared at me over the guitar.

“Jasper.”

“I'm trying to narrow down the possibilities.”

He looked down at the receipt. “I just don't want to finish it wrong.”

I sat on the edge of the pier beside him. For a while I watched a gull negotiate with a paper bag. It was losing, which struck me as an important lesson about ambition.

“What's a wrong ending?” I asked.

He played two notes, then stopped. “A song that makes it sound like we've figured everything out.”

“We haven't.”

“Right. But if I write it down, it starts looking permanent.”

I knew that feeling. A promise spoken in a good moment could become a cage if nobody was allowed to revisit it. I had learned that love needed room for questions. We had both made too many assumptions in other relationships to pretend otherwise.

“So let's write the questions,” I said.

Greg raised his eyebrows. “That is not a traditional chorus.”

“Neither is brake fluid.”

He grinned. I moved closer and pointed to the third line.

“Try the chord you played yesterday.”

“That one was weird.”

“It was honest.”

“Those aren't always the same thing.”

“Today they can be.”

He let me hold the notebook while he tuned. His fingers were rough from strings and work, familiar in a way that still surprised me when I noticed it. I'd come to Beach City thinking I could keep one foot outside every doorway. Somehow I was here, worrying about whether a little song sounded too much like home.

We tried the phrase again.

This time I sang the part he had been avoiding. My voice cracked on the higher note.

Greg kept playing.

“That was terrible,” I said when we finished.

“That was alive,” he replied.

“Same thing, apparently.”

He laughed, but then he stopped.

“Can I ask you something without making it a whole big thing?”

“Probably. But that phrasing guarantees it'll become one.”

He set the guitar down between us, his hands resting lightly on the strings.

“When you tell me you want room for other relationships, I believe you. I'm not trying to change your mind.” He swallowed. “Sometimes I get scared you'll hear a better song somewhere and forget this one.”

There it was.

Not a theory about love. Not an argument about whether polyamory worked. A person I cared about, telling me what frightened him without dressing it up as a punch line.

“I can't promise I'll never change,” I said.

“I know.”

“And I won't promise to want only one person. I've been honest about that from the start.”

“I know.”

“But I can promise not to disappear without telling you the truth about where we stand. I can promise to check in. I can promise to listen if something hurts.”

He nodded once, looking down at his hands.

“I think that's what I needed.”

“Then why did you make me listen to three versions of the same chorus before saying it?”

He looked up. “I was hoping you'd be distracted by my musical genius.”

“That works more often than you realize.”

Greg laughed so hard he nearly dropped the notebook.

We moved to the car wash when the wind rose. The place was closed, and the little plywood stage stood empty beneath the striped awning. Greg brought out a battered speaker and a pair of old stools. I sat on the less alarming one. He sat on the stool that leaned to the left.

“You could get a new chair,” I said.

“You could stop insulting my furniture.”

“I'm committed to this relationship, not the chair.”

He pressed a hand to his chest. “Finally. A reasonable boundary.”

We recorded the verse twice.

On the first take, a passing truck drowned out the final note. On the second, the speaker buzzed so badly that Greg apologized to it. The third was imperfect for a different reason: I started laughing halfway through because he made a face at the wrong moment.

He played the recording back.

I sounded nervous and warm. He sounded a little rough around the edges. Neither of us sounded like a person performing certainty.

“I like it,” he said.

“That's because you like me.”

“That's true.” He paused. “I like the song too.”

He copied the clean version onto a proper sheet of paper. At the top he wrote two names.

I stared.

“You didn't have to put mine there.”

“You wrote half the second verse.”

“I changed two lines.”

“Two pretty important lines.”

I took the pencil. Beneath our names I wrote: SUBJECT TO REVISION.

He read it and smiled.

“Now that's a title.”

“No. That's the warning label.”

“Even better.”

Later Steven called. Greg talked about work, the weather, and the fact that a seagull had tried to steal our dinner. He told Steven we were writing together, but he did not turn our relationship into a grand announcement. When he hung up, he seemed lighter.

“You okay?” I asked.

“Yeah. I think I am.”

He pulled me into a gentle kiss, unhurried enough for us both to change our minds and neither of us wanting to. The guitar rested against the chair. The recording waited on the little player, full of wrong notes we had decided to keep.

We went back to the van while the last boardwalk lights blinked off. He opened the door and offered me his hand, suddenly a little shy.

“Stay for another song?” he asked.

I took his hand.

“Only if you promise not to make me rhyme with ‘star.’”

“No promises.”

We let the rest of the night remain ours.

In the morning the receipt was still on the dashboard, folded around the battery list. The new sheet of music sat safely in the glove compartment.

Greg put a fresh date in the corner.

“Why?” I asked.

“Because we're going to keep changing it.”

I leaned over and kissed his cheek.

For the first time, finishing the song didn't feel like closing a door.

It felt like leaving it unlocked for the next verse.
